newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel passes product liability bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel passes product liability bill.

text.p: The Senate Commerce Committee Thursday approved a bill to limit damages in product liability lawsuits, but opponents said it was likely to be vetoed again by President Clinton.

The bill would limit punitive damages in product liability cases to twice the compensatory damages or $250,000, whichever is greater. Clinton vetoed a similar bill last year, saying it went too far in curbing the rights of injury victims.
The bill passed on an 11-9 party line vote, with all the panel's Republicans voting for it and all Democrats opposed.
Sen. Slade Gorton, a Washington Republican and the bill's author, said excessive liability damages and frivolous lawsuits were raising prices and discouraging development of new products.
Gorton said defendents often have to wait years for suits to be tried and those who win must give much of their award to lawyers. "We have a system that does not do justice to anyone," he said.

But Sen. Ernest Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat, said reforms were not needed. He said product liability cases made up less than one percent of all U.S. lawsuits and the number of excessive awards had been exaggerated.
"Product liability works. It's not a national problem," Hollings said. He said Congress should let states deal with tort law issues. "Here we go again with an unconstitutional measure," he added.

Gorton said his bill had been changed from last year's version to overcome many of Clinton's objections. Supporters of liability limits last year said they believed Clinton vetoed the bill because of the large campaign contributions he got from trial lawyers, who strongly oppose the legislation.

The committee's action came as the full Senate continued to debate a separate bill to protect volunteers and non-profit groups from lawsuits for negligence. Democrats have been blocking a vote on that bill.
